title: Rabbit cage floor options
subtitle: The welfare and practical trade-offs between wire, slatted, and solid-floored rabbit housing.
excerpt: The floor is the single most debated aspect of rabbit housing design. Wire mesh floors allow urine and droppings to fall through, keeping the rabbit clean and reducing disease pressure, but wire that is too light or widely spaced causes foot damage. Solid floors need daily cleaning but are warmer and more natural underfoot. Understanding the trade-offs helps you choose a setup that balances welfare, hygiene, and your management time.

glossaryTerms.definition: Ulcerative pododermatitis: a painful condition where the skin and tissue over the hock joint (the equivalent of the human heel) breaks down from prolonged contact with a hard or abrasive surface, urine, or faeces. Most common in large or heavy breeds on wire mesh or bare wire floors.

Skin damage caused by prolonged contact between urine and the skin of the hindquarters or feet. Common in rabbits on soiled solid floors or in cages where urine cannot drain away. Affected skin appears red, hairless, and inflamed.

content.text: Floor type in rabbit housing determines how clean the cage stays, how much labour the keeper puts in, and whether the rabbit develops foot problems. There is no single right answer: what works depends on the breed, the stocking density, the climate, and how often the housing is cleaned.
Wire mesh floors

Wire mesh allows urine and faeces to fall through into a drop tray or onto the ground, keeping the rabbit off its own waste. This significantly reduces coccidiosis pressure and urine scald risk and is the standard in commercial meat rabbit production. The welfare risks of wire floors come from inadequate specification:
Mesh must be galvanised welded wire, minimum 16 gauge, with openings no larger than 25 mm by 13 mm. Lighter wire bends under weight and creates sharp protruding ends.
Large or heavy breeds (Flemish Giant, New Zealand White over 5 kg) are at significant risk of
sore hocks
on wire mesh. These breeds benefit from a solid resting board (a tile, a timber board, or a plastic mat) in part of the cage.
All rabbits on wire floors should have a resting mat or platform where they can sit with all four feet on a solid surface for at least part of the day.
Solid floors with bedding
A solid-floored hutch, run, or cage needs bedding changed frequently. The key welfare risk is
urine scald
in wet or soiled corners. Good bedding choices:
Kiln-dried, dust-extracted wood shavings: absorb urine well and are easy to clean.
Straw: good insulation in winter, poor absorbency; better as a top layer over shavings than as a sole bedding.
Paper-based pellet bedding: absorbs well and produces very low dust, but costs more than shavings.
Cedar shavings: avoid entirely. Cedar oils are toxic to small animals.
Slatted floors

Slatted floors made from smooth plastic or hard rubber provide drainage without the foot-injury risk of wire. They are easier on the hock for heavy breeds. The slots need to be wide enough to allow faeces to fall through (typically 10 to 15 mm) but not so wide that feet catch. Plastic slats are easier to disinfect than wire or timber.
Practical recommendation

For most smallholder rabbits (medium to large breed, individually or pair housed), a hybrid approach works well: two thirds of the cage floor as 16-gauge welded wire mesh for waste management, with a solid timber or rubber resting board on one third. This gives drainage and hygiene without constant foot-to-wire contact.

The RWAF and RSPCA both recommend that all domestic rabbits have access to at least one solid-floored resting area regardless of the overall cage floor type. Rabbits spend significant time sitting still; prolonged contact with any hard surface without padding contributes to hock problems over months and years.
